questions.stem: Where did most of the gases in Earth's early atmosphere, after its first atmosphere was lost, come from?
options: Evaporation of the oceans, which released mostly free oxygen gas
Capture of hydrogen and helium from the solar wind over time
Volcanic outgassing of water vapour, carbon dioxide and nitrogen
Photosynthesis by early plants releasing large amounts of oxygen
questions.explanation: Gases released by volcanic activity, mainly water vapour, carbon dioxide and nitrogen, built up Earth's early atmosphere, which had almost no free oxygen. Photosynthesis added oxygen much later, after cyanobacteria evolved, and land plants came later still.

questions.stem: Astronomers estimate the young Sun was about 30 per cent fainter than today, yet rocks show liquid water on Earth more than 3.5 billion years ago. Which explanation is most widely accepted?
options: The oceans were frozen at the surface and liquid only around volcanoes
A thick ozone layer absorbed sunlight and warmed the surface directly
Higher greenhouse gas levels, such as carbon dioxide, trapped more heat
Earth was much closer to the Sun and later moved out to its present orbit
questions.explanation: An early atmosphere rich in carbon dioxide, and possibly methane, gave a much stronger greenhouse effect that kept water liquid despite the fainter Sun. There was no ozone layer before free oxygen accumulated, and there is no evidence that Earth's orbit has moved outwards.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide made up a large share of Earth's early atmosphere but is now a trace gas. Where did most of that carbon go?
options: Into space, because carbon dioxide molecules are light enough to escape
Into the inner core, where it was carried by sinking iron-rich material
Into the stratosphere, where it was converted to ozone by sunlight
Into carbonate rocks such as limestone, after dissolving in seawater
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans and was locked away in carbonate sediments, later aided by organisms building shells and by burial of organic carbon. Carbon dioxide is far too heavy to escape to space, and the core does not store atmospheric carbon.

questions.stem: Which list gives the three most abundant gases in modern dry air, from most to least abundant?
options: Nitrogen, carbon dioxide, oxygen
Nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide
Nitrogen, oxygen, argon
Oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Dry air is about 78 per cent nitrogen, 21 per cent oxygen and just under 1 per cent argon. Carbon dioxide is a trace gas at well under 0.1 per cent, despite its importance for climate.

questions.stem: Proxy data indicate that in the Cretaceous Period atmospheric carbon dioxide was several times higher than before the industrial era, there were no large polar ice sheets and sea level was much higher. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Carbon dioxide has no effect on climate because ice sheets control sea level
A carbon-rich atmosphere is linked to a warm, ice-free 'greenhouse' climate
High sea levels caused the high carbon dioxide by releasing it from the ocean
The Sun must have been much brighter in the Cretaceous than it is today
questions.explanation: Periods with high carbon dioxide in the geological record coincide with warm climates, little polar ice and high sea levels, consistent with a stronger greenhouse effect. The Sun has slowly brightened over time, so it was slightly fainter, not brighter, in the Cretaceous.

questions.stem: Why does Earth's surface emit mostly infrared radiation, while the Sun emits mostly visible and near-infrared radiation?
options: Earth's surface is far cooler, and cooler bodies radiate at longer wavelengths
Earth's atmosphere converts all incoming visible light into infrared radiation
Earth's surface reflects the infrared part of sunlight and absorbs the rest
Earth's surface is denser than the Sun, so it radiates at longer wavelengths
questions.explanation: The wavelength at which a body radiates most strongly depends on its temperature: the Sun's surface is about 5500 degrees Celsius, while Earth's surface averages about 15 degrees Celsius, so Earth radiates in the infrared. The atmosphere transmits most visible light rather than converting it.

questions.stem: Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 per cent of dry air, yet they contribute almost nothing to the greenhouse effect. Why?
options: They absorb infrared strongly but re-emit all of it straight to space
They are found only in the upper atmosphere, above most radiation
Molecules of two identical atoms barely absorb infrared radiation
They are too abundant to absorb infrared, since the air is saturated
questions.explanation: Molecules such as N2 and O2 have no change in charge distribution when they vibrate, so they hardly absorb infrared radiation. Molecules with three or more atoms, such as H2O, CO2 and CH4, have vibrations that do absorb infrared, which makes them greenhouse gases.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how greenhouse gases warm the lower atmosphere and surface?
options: They absorb infrared from the surface and re-emit it in all directions, some back down
They absorb incoming visible sunlight and pass the energy directly to the oceans
They reflect infrared from the surface back down, as a glass mirror reflects light
They block incoming ultraviolet radiation, which stops it from cooling the surface
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gas molecules absorb infrared radiation emitted by the surface and then re-emit energy in every direction, so part returns to warm the surface and lower atmosphere. This is absorption and re-emission, not reflection, and greenhouse gases are largely transparent to incoming visible light.

questions.stem: Which group contains only greenhouse gases?
options: Argon, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide
Oxygen, carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour
Water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide
Water vapour, carbon dioxide, nitrogen, nitrous oxide
questions.explanation: Water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide all absorb infrared radiation and are greenhouse gases. Nitrogen, oxygen and argon do not absorb infrared significantly.

questions.stem: The global warming potential (GWP) of a gas compares:
options: the amount of the gas in the atmosphere with the amount of CO2 in the atmosphere
the temperature at which the gas absorbs infrared with the temperature for CO2
the warming from a mass of the gas over a set time with that of the same mass of CO2
the warming from a mass of the gas in one year with that of the same mass of methane
questions.explanation: GWP is the heat trapped by a given mass of a gas over a chosen period, usually 100 years, relative to the same mass of carbon dioxide, whose GWP is 1. It measures warming per unit mass, not how much of the gas is present.

questions.stem: Methane's GWP over 20 years is much higher than its GWP over 100 years. Why?
options: Methane turns into nitrous oxide after 20 years, which has a much lower warming effect
Most methane is removed within a few decades, so its effect is diluted over 100 years
Methane absorbs more infrared each year it stays in the air, so its effect grows
Carbon dioxide is removed faster than methane, so over 20 years methane looks stronger
questions.explanation: Methane traps heat strongly but lasts only about a decade in the atmosphere, while added carbon dioxide persists for centuries. Averaged over 100 years, methane's warming is spread over many years in which most of it has already gone, so its GWP is lower than over 20 years.

questions.stem: Using a 100-year GWP of 265 for nitrous oxide, what are the carbon dioxide equivalent emissions of a farm releasing 3 tonnes of nitrous oxide a year?
options: 268 tonnes CO2-e per year
88 tonnes CO2-e per year
530 tonnes CO2-e per year
795 tonnes CO2-e per year
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide equivalent is the mass of the gas multiplied by its GWP: 3 x 265 = 795 tonnes. Adding the two numbers gives 268, and using only 2 tonnes gives 530.

questions.stem: A synthetic gas absorbs infrared strongly at wavelengths where water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb very little, and it stays in the atmosphere for thousands of years. What would you expect of its GWP?
options: Very low, since a gas that lasts so long is spread too thinly to matter
Close to 1, since all long-lived gases warm about as much as CO2 does
Very high, since both strong absorption and a long lifespan raise GWP
Very low, since it absorbs at wavelengths that cannot warm the surface
questions.explanation: GWP rises with how strongly a gas absorbs infrared, especially in the 'atmospheric window' where other gases absorb little, and with how long it stays in the air. Gases with both features, such as sulfur hexafluoride, have GWPs thousands of times that of carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Water vapour is the largest contributor to the natural greenhouse effect, yet it is not given a GWP and is not counted as a cause of climate change. Why?
options: It stays in the air only days and its amount is set by temperature, so it acts as a feedback
It does not absorb infrared radiation, so it only affects clouds and the reflection of sunlight
It is removed from the air within days, so it has no effect at all on surface temperature
It is produced only by natural processes, and GWP is used only for gases made by humans
questions.explanation: Water vapour stays in the atmosphere for only about nine days, and warmer air holds more of it, so its concentration follows temperature. It therefore amplifies warming started by other causes rather than driving it. It is a strong infrared absorber, so it certainly does affect surface temperature.

questions.stem: Which part of incoming solar radiation is mostly absorbed in the stratosphere before reaching the ground?
options: Visible light, absorbed by nitrogen
Infrared, which is absorbed by argon
Radio waves, absorbed by oxygen
Ultraviolet, which is absorbed by ozone
questions.explanation: Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs most incoming ultraviolet radiation, which warms that layer. Most visible light passes through the clear atmosphere to the surface, and nitrogen and argon absorb very little solar radiation.

questions.stem: A surface with an albedo of 0.6 receives 200 W/m2 of sunlight. How much of this energy does it absorb?
questions.explanation: Albedo is the fraction reflected, so 0.6 x 200 = 120 W/m2 is reflected and 200 - 120 = 80 W/m2 is absorbed. Giving 120 W/m2 mistakes the reflected part for the absorbed part.

questions.stem: Small changes in Earth's orbit begin to cool summers at high northern latitudes, and snow starts to last through the year. Why can this lead to a much larger cooling than the orbital change alone would cause?
options: Growing ice lowers albedo, so more sunlight is reflected and cooling is amplified
Growing ice raises albedo, so less sunlight is absorbed and cooling is amplified
Growing ice releases heat as it freezes, so the atmosphere above it cools faster
Growing ice absorbs carbon dioxide directly, so the greenhouse effect switches off
questions.explanation: Ice and snow reflect much more sunlight than land or sea, so expanding ice cover reduces absorbed energy and causes more cooling, a positive feedback. A lower albedo would mean less reflection, not more. Freezing actually releases latent heat, which slows rather than speeds cooling.

questions.stem: Which type of cloud tends to have an overall warming effect on Earth's surface?
options: Thick, low sea fog banks
High, thin cirrus cloud
Low, thick stratus cloud
Bright, low cumulus cloud
questions.explanation: High, thin cirrus lets most sunlight through but absorbs infrared from below and, being cold, emits little to space, so it warms overall. Low, thick clouds reflect a lot of sunlight and have a net cooling effect.

questions.stem: Earth's average temperature is stable when the energy it absorbs from the Sun equals the energy it emits as infrared. What happens if Earth's albedo decreases?
options: It warms without limit, since nothing can increase the infrared lost
It stays the same, since albedo affects only the infrared it emits
It warms until it emits enough extra infrared to balance the gain
It cools until it absorbs enough extra sunlight to balance the loss
questions.explanation: A lower albedo means more sunlight is absorbed, so Earth gains energy and warms. A warmer surface emits more infrared, so it reaches a new, higher balance temperature rather than warming without limit.

questions.stem: Milankovitch cycles are long-term changes in:
options: the number of sunspots and the total energy radiated by the Sun's surface
the arrangement of continents and the size of the ocean basins between them
the strength of Earth's magnetic field and the speed of Earth's rotation
the shape of Earth's orbit, the tilt of its axis and the wobble of the axis
questions.explanation: Milankovitch cycles are eccentricity (orbit shape), obliquity (axial tilt) and precession (the wobble of the axis), which change how sunlight is spread across latitudes and seasons. Sunspot cycles are a separate solar effect.

questions.stem: Earth's axial tilt (obliquity) varies between about 22 and 24.5 degrees. Over roughly what period does it complete one cycle?
options: About 11 years
About 1000 years
About 400 million years
About 41 000 years
questions.explanation: Obliquity varies on a cycle of about 41 000 years. Eccentricity varies on a cycle of about 100 000 years, and the axial wobble (precession) takes about 26 000 years. Eleven years is the sunspot cycle.

questions.stem: When Earth's axial tilt is near its maximum, what happens to the seasons at high latitudes?
options: Both summers and winters become warmer
The seasons are unchanged, as tilt is fixed
Summers become warmer and winters colder
Summers become cooler and winters warmer
questions.explanation: A larger tilt points each pole more directly at the Sun in its summer and further away in its winter, so seasonal contrast increases. A smaller tilt gives milder seasons, with cooler summers that let snow survive and favour ice-sheet growth.

questions.stem: Which combination of orbital conditions is most likely to allow ice sheets to grow on the large land masses of the high northern latitudes?
options: Low tilt, with northern winter occurring when Earth is furthest from the Sun
High tilt, with northern winter occurring when Earth is closest to the Sun
Low tilt, with northern summer occurring when Earth is furthest from the Sun
High tilt, with northern summer occurring when Earth is closest to the Sun
questions.explanation: Ice sheets grow when summers are cool enough for winter snow to survive. A low tilt and a northern summer at the far point of the orbit both reduce summer sunlight at high northern latitudes. Cold winters matter less, because summer melting controls whether snow accumulates.

questions.stem: Ice cores show glacial and interglacial periods alternating roughly every 100 000 years, yet orbital changes alter the total sunlight Earth receives in a year by only a tiny amount. How is this best explained?
options: Orbital changes alter where and when sunlight falls, and feedbacks amplify the change
Orbital changes are too small to matter, so glacial cycles must be caused by sunspots
Orbital changes alter the total sunlight greatly, so no feedbacks are needed at all
Orbital changes trigger volcanic eruptions, and their ash causes each glacial period
questions.explanation: Milankovitch cycles mainly redistribute sunlight between seasons and latitudes. Changes in ice-albedo and in greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide released from or taken up by the oceans, then amplify the small initial change into a full glacial or interglacial shift.

questions.stem: When the number of sunspots is high, the Sun's total energy output is:
options: unchanged, since sunspots affect only the Sun's magnetic field
slightly higher, as bright areas around the spots outweigh them
much lower, since the dark spots block a large part of the light
slightly lower, since the dark spots are cooler than the surface
questions.explanation: Sunspots are dark, but they come with bright regions called faculae, so overall the Sun emits slightly more energy at sunspot maximum. The difference over a cycle is only about 0.1 per cent.

questions.stem: The number of sunspots rises and falls in a cycle that lasts on average about:
options: 1 year
11 years
41 years
100 years
questions.explanation: Sunspot numbers peak and fall roughly every 11 years. Longer periods of low activity, such as the Maunder Minimum, also occur.

questions.stem: The Maunder Minimum, a period from about 1645 to 1715 with very few sunspots, overlapped one of the coldest parts of the Little Ice Age in Europe. What is the most valid conclusion?
options: Solar activity cannot affect climate, because the Little Ice Age began well before the Maunder Minimum
Cold European weather caused the low sunspot numbers by blocking the view of the Sun with cloud
Low solar activity may have contributed, but other causes such as volcanic eruptions must be considered
Low solar activity was the only cause of the Little Ice Age, since the two events happened together
questions.explanation: A correlation is consistent with a solar influence but does not prove it was the only cause. Large volcanic eruptions and natural ocean variability occurred in the same centuries, so scientists weigh several factors together.

questions.stem: Total solar output changes by only about 0.1 per cent over a sunspot cycle. What does this suggest about sunspot cycles and climate?
options: They have no measurable link to any variation in temperature
They cause small, short-lived changes in global temperature
They cause the full change between glacial and interglacial
They cause large temperature swings every eleven years or so
questions.explanation: A 0.1 per cent change in solar output is small and reverses within about 11 years, so it produces only slight, temporary changes in global temperature. Glacial cycles are linked to orbital changes amplified by feedbacks.

questions.stem: The plate-tectonic supercycle is:
options: the yearly movement of plates of a few centimetres at spreading ridges and trenches
the build-up and release of stress along a fault that causes repeated earthquakes
the eruption cycle of hot-spot volcanoes as a plate moves over a mantle plume
the repeated joining and break-up of supercontinents over hundreds of millions of years
questions.explanation: The supercycle describes continents gathering into a supercontinent, such as Pangaea, which later rifts apart before the continents gather again. Each cycle takes several hundred million years and affects sea level, ocean currents and climate.

questions.stem: When a supercontinent breaks apart, many new spreading ridges form. How does this tend to affect global climate?
options: More volcanic CO2 and higher sea levels give a warmer climate
Less volcanic CO2 and lower sea levels give a cooler climate
More volcanic CO2 and lower sea levels give a cooler climate
Less volcanic CO2 and higher sea levels give a warmer climate
questions.explanation: Active spreading ridges release carbon dioxide and, being hot and buoyant, take up volume in the ocean basins, which raises sea level. Together these favour warm 'greenhouse' periods, such as the Cretaceous after Pangaea broke up.

questions.stem: As Australia and South America moved away from Antarctica, deep ocean gateways opened and a current began to flow all the way around Antarctica. How did this help Antarctica's ice sheet to form?
options: The circling current kept warm tropical water away, cooling Antarctica
The circling current carried warm water south, adding snowfall to Antarctica
The circling current raised sea level, flooding Antarctica with cold water
The circling current blocked the westerly winds, so Antarctica lost heat
questions.explanation: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current isolates Antarctica from warmer waters further north, reducing heat transport to the continent and helping a permanent ice sheet to grow. This shows how plate movements alter climate by changing ocean circulation.

questions.stem: The uplift of large mountain ranges such as the Himalaya is thought to have contributed to long-term cooling. Through which process?
options: Faster growth of mountain forests, which adds methane to the air
Faster weathering of silicate rocks, which removes CO2 from the air
Faster eruption of volcanoes, which adds reflective ash to the air
Faster melting of mountain glaciers, which adds fresh water to seas
questions.explanation: Freshly exposed rock in high, wet mountains weathers chemically, and the reactions consume carbon dioxide, which is eventually locked into ocean carbonate sediments. Volcanic ash cools climate only for a year or two, not over millions of years.

questions.stem: The specific heat capacity of a substance is the energy needed to:
options: raise the temperature of 1 kg of it to boiling
change 1 kg of it from a liquid into a gas
raise the temperature of 1 kg of it by 1 degree
change 1 kg of it from a solid into a liquid
questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 kelvin (1 degree Celsius). The energy for changes of state is latent heat, a different quantity.

questions.stem: Water has a specific heat capacity of about 4200 J/kg/K and dry sand about 840 J/kg/K. If 1 kg of each absorbs 42 000 J, by how much does each warm?
options: Water by 50 degrees, sand by 10 degrees
Water by 10 degrees, sand by 20 degrees
Both by 10 degrees, as the energy is equal
Water by 10 degrees, sand by 50 degrees
questions.explanation: Temperature change is energy divided by (mass x specific heat capacity): 42 000 / 4200 = 10 degrees for water and 42 000 / 840 = 50 degrees for sand. Equal energy does not give equal warming when heat capacities differ.

questions.stem: A coastal town and an inland town at the same latitude receive the same sunlight. Why does the coastal town have a smaller range between summer and winter temperatures?
options: The nearby ocean reflects most sunlight, so the town receives less energy
The nearby ocean adds greenhouse gases only in winter, warming the town
The nearby ocean absorbs heat only in summer and never releases it again
The nearby ocean warms and cools slowly because of its high heat capacity
questions.explanation: Water needs a lot of energy to change temperature, and the ocean mixes heat through a deep layer, so it stays cooler than land in summer and warmer in winter, moderating nearby air temperatures. Open ocean actually reflects little sunlight because of its low albedo.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts surface and deep-water ocean currents?
options: Surface currents are driven mainly by tides; deep currents by the Earth's rotation
Surface currents are driven mainly by rivers; deep currents by undersea volcanoes
Surface currents are driven mainly by wind; deep currents by density differences
Surface currents are driven mainly by density; deep currents by the trade winds
questions.explanation: Winds blowing across the sea drag the upper few hundred metres into motion, forming surface currents. Deep currents are driven by differences in water density caused by temperature and salinity, the thermohaline circulation.

questions.stem: The strong westerly wind belt of the Southern Ocean drives which current?
options: The westward current along the equator
The southward East Australian Current
The northward deep current of the Atlantic
The eastward Antarctic Circumpolar Current
questions.explanation: The westerlies blow from west to east around the Southern Ocean, and with no continents in the way they drive the Antarctic Circumpolar Current eastward around Antarctica. Westward equatorial currents are driven by the trade winds.

questions.stem: In the Southern Hemisphere, the large surface current loops (gyres) of the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans circulate in which direction, and why?
options: Anticlockwise, steered by the trade winds, westerlies and Coriolis effect
Clockwise, steered by the trade winds, westerlies and Coriolis effect
Anticlockwise, steered by density differences between warm and cold water
Clockwise, steered by the tides raised by the Moon and the Sun each day
questions.explanation: Trade winds push water west near the equator and westerlies push it east at higher latitudes; deflection to the left by the Coriolis effect completes an anticlockwise loop in the Southern Hemisphere. Northern Hemisphere gyres turn clockwise.

questions.stem: Water sampled at 3000 m depth in the North Pacific is low in dissolved oxygen but rich in dissolved CO2 and nutrients. Which explanation fits the thermohaline circulation?
options: It is young surface water that has just sunk, carrying oxygen-poor air down from the atmosphere
It is water warmed by undersea volcanoes, which drives oxygen out and adds nutrients from rock
It is fresh water from melting ice, which carries few gases and nutrients down into the depths
It is old deep water that left the surface long ago, while decay used oxygen and released CO2
questions.explanation: Deep water forms at high latitudes and travels slowly for centuries before reaching the North Pacific. Along the way it has no contact with the air, while sinking organic matter decomposes, using oxygen and adding carbon dioxide and nutrients.
